summary: Build report pages bespoke and with soft-ui, then judge each pair blind for intent match

a_only: KPI tiles with totals (8 tables, 36 columns, 8 foreign keys, 2.1M rows)
A separate foreign-key table (from table, FK column, points to, nullable), grouped by table
A treemap of each table's share of all rows, coloured by index count
Per-table counts of columns, foreign keys and nullable columns in the summary table
One flat table of all 36 columns, with a search box and filters by table and key
b_only: Conventions card (uuid keys, money as integer cents, status enums)
A 'watch for' card: orders.address_id and placed_at can be null
A dashed line in the ER diagram for a nullable FK, row counts on each diagram table, and hover to trace links
Bars for both disk size and rows, with a percent of disk for the top three tables
A plain-language description of each table and what it is for
Links on each table card to the tables it points to and the tables that reference it
A warning that order_discounts has no primary key, so the same code can be applied twice
judge.why: B explains what each table means and points out the traps that a new engineer would miss: the missing primary key, the nullable foreign keys and the conventions. A has more ways to count and filter the data, but these suit someone who already knows the schema better than a first-week reader.

bespoke.notes: The page opens with four key facts: orders is the hub, three tables hold about 97% of the data, the column conventions, and the warnings (order_discounts has no primary key, and some fields in orders can be null). Next is a hand-placed SVG diagram of all eight tables that uses crow's-foot links, shows nullable foreign keys as dashed lines, and lights up a table's links on hover. Last come linear size and row bars sorted by size, then one detail card per table in data-flow order, with links to the tables it points to and the tables that point to it.

error_lines: error data.tables.sort: no column "rows". Columns: table, count, fk, null_ok
error layout[3].section[1].table: no dataset "tables". Datasets: schema, stats, fks
tool.friction: 1) stats.csv stores size as human text ("38 MB", "1.2 GB", "64 kB"). Expressions do not allow subscripts or string methods, so I could not parse size to bytes. A test render with treemap size: size, fmt: bytes passed "check ok" but showed no error. The page probably got wrong values (parseFloat gives 1.2 for "1.2 GB"), and the check did not catch it. So the size charts use row count, and disk size appears only as a text column. A bytes parser for "NN MB/GB" strings, or a warning when a numeric prop gets unit strings, would help. 2) Dataset steps run in a fixed order: join comes before group. My first spec had group then join in one dataset, and the error ("no column rows") did not say that join runs before group. I split it into two datasets (percol, then tables from percol). A hint such as "join runs before group; use from: to join after" would have saved a render. 3) A table-to-table relation graph needs the referenced table name, but references holds "customers.id". No string split exists, so I relied on the er diagram for the relations and did not use graph. 4) Expression errors in data.add cascade into "no dataset" errors on every node that uses the dataset, which adds noise. 5) I could not check the page visually (no playwright in this environment), so I relied on render's "check ok". I wrote the callout text by hand from reading the schema (orders is the hub, order_discounts has no primary key), and it does not come from the data.

a_only: A headline summary that gives the answer first: web and core hold 54% of the lines, there is one cycle, and five large files change often
Paired bars that compare each module's share of lines with its share of commits, with a note that billing changes 3 times more often than its size predicts
Infra shown in the graph as a node with no import edges, plus a note that infra can be refactored alone
Written findings beside the graph: core carries the most load (81 imports), web to shared is the heaviest edge, and how to break the cycle
A table of all 10 import edges, with the two cycle edges highlighted
A separate class in the scatter for small files with very high churn (billing/handlers/f01.go, billing/service/f02.go, billing/views/f00.go, web/util/f22.tsx), with a note about each
A note on large files that did not change (jobs/util/f02.py, core/model/f05.go and others)
A top-12 table ranked by lines x commits, with a type tag for each file (large and changes often, or very high churn)
A shaded quadrant for large files that change often, with each file labelled in the scatter
The threshold is 400+ lines and 8+ commits, which gives 5 candidate files
b_only: KPI tiles for the number of source files (141) and total commits (745)
A cycle callout above the first chart that says api and jobs reach the cycle through billing
A bar chart of lines of code by module, shown next to the treemap
A module table with the file count, lines, share of code and commits of each module
An import matrix heatmap (from row to column) beside the node graph
A table of only the two cycle edges
Scatter dots coloured by module
The threshold is 300+ lines and 8+ commits, which gives 8 candidate files (adds web/service/f12.tsx, web/service/f01.tsx and web/views/f05.tsx)
A folded 'All files' table with all 141 files
judge.why: Page A (bespoke.html) tells the tech lead what to do at each step. It compares each module's share of lines with its share of change, explains the cycle and how to break it, and separates large files that change often from small files with very high churn. Page B (tool.html) shows the same core views (treemap, import graph, scatter, candidate table) and some extra raw views, but it leaves most of the reading to the tech lead and leaves infra out of the import graph.

bespoke.notes: The page opens with the answer and 4 KPI tiles (web and core hold 54% of the lines, 1 cycle between core and billing, 5 large files that change often). Hand-built SVG sections follow: a squarified treemap of files by module (area is lines, color is commits), paired bars that compare each module's share of lines with its share of commits (billing is 7.6% of lines but 23% of commits), a layered dependency graph with the core and billing cycle in red next to a list of the import edges, and a scatter of lines against commits with the high-risk corner shaded and a top-12 ranked table.

error_lines: error data.edges.add: add.pair: "from + '>' + to" is not a valid expression
error data.edges.add: add.rev: "to + '>' + from" is not a valid expression
error data.cycles: from: no dataset "edges" above this one. Datasets: files, imports, scored, modules
error layout[0].row[3].stat: no dataset "cycles". Datasets: files, imports, scored, modules, hot
error data.cycles.where: no column "back". Columns: src, dst, imports, pair, rev
error layout[0].row[3].stat: no dataset "cycles". Datasets: files, imports, scored, modules, links, edges, reverse, hot
tool.friction:
The import cycle was the hardest part. No dataset step or graph prop finds cycles, so I built one from 5 chained datasets: rename, add pair/rev keys, rename imports to back, a self-join, then a filter. Five problems came up on the way:
(1) The column name "from" in imports.csv cannot appear in an `add` expression (it is a Python keyword), and the error says only "not a valid expression". I renamed the columns in a separate dataset as a workaround.
(2) The steps run in a fixed order (where, join, add, ...), so `add` columns cannot be used in a `join` or `where` of the same dataset. No error is printed for this: the first join quietly matched nothing. I needed extra datasets.
(3) BUG: `where: {back: ">0"}` keeps rows where back is null after a left join. All 10 edges passed the filter, but only 2 should have. The page said "check ok", so a wrong stat value would have shipped silently. Workaround: add {in_cycle: "'yes' if back else 'no'"}, then where in_cycle: yes.
(4) The graph component cannot highlight the cycle edges or nodes. `tone` works only on node attributes, and there is no edge tone. The cycle therefore shows only in a callout and a small table. The callout numbers (22, 4) are typed by hand.
(5) BUG: in a scatter chart, `mark: [{x: 300}]` draws the vertical line near x=0, not at 300. The y-mark at 8 is correct.
Other points: a row of 5 stat tiles wrapped the 5th tile onto its own line until I set min: 150. The treemap legend shows the raw column name "commits_90d", and the scatter axis titles use raw column names; I found no labels prop for them. The table `labels` prop works.
I wanted a "hot file" quadrant (a shaded band for 300+ lines and 8+ commits) on the scatter, and I could not draw it.
The shared scratchpad screenshot path was overwritten by another agent's page, which looked like the bespoke version. I saw it only by accident and re-shot to a unique file name. A per-run default --shot name would prevent this.

a_only: KPI tiles that count the blocks in each voltage domain (3V0 1, 3V3 6, 1V8 2, RF 1)
Block nodes colour-coded by kind (power, compute, sensor, output, radio), with a text key
Links table grouped into folded sections for 'crosses domain' (4) and 'same domain' (6), with from_domain and to_domain columns
Truth table shades every chirp=1 and led=1 cell, not only the alarm rows
Links table comes after the truth table
b_only: KPI tiles for the link count by type and '3 of 16 input cases raise the alarm'
Diagram legend for the line types (power rail, GPIO/PWM, I2C bus, RF), MCU pin labels (P0.11, P0.12, P0.20, P0.13, TWI, ANT), and a marked level shifter (LS) on the I2C crossing
Text that says the I2C bus is the only signal that crosses domains
Links table with a Type column (Power/Bus/GPIO/RF), notes for regulator and RF path, and a red flag on the level-shifted I2C crossing
Expression cards that give the true-case count for each output (3, 4, and 12 of 16)
Row numbers 0-15, with INPUTS and OUTPUTS column groups
Interactive 'Try one case' panel that sets the inputs and shows the outputs, with a plain-language reason
'What the table shows' bullets: the alarm rows, the override effect, chirp and alarm never true together, and firmware hints about PIR and IRQ
judge.why: Both pages give the block diagram with domains, the full 16-row truth table with the alarm rows marked, and the links table. B serves the new firmware engineer better: it shows the MCU pins, the bus types, and the level shifter on the diagram, and it explains what the truth table means for the firmware.

bespoke.notes: The page opens with a hand-placed inline SVG block diagram. Each voltage domain (3V0, 3V3, 1V8, RF) is a shaded area, and each link type has its own line style: power rail, GPIO/PWM, I2C bus and RF. The MCU pins are labelled, and an LS marker shows where the I2C bus crosses from 1V8 to 3V3. Below the diagram are a connections table and the full 16-row truth table, computed from logic.json, with the 3 alarm rows (10, 12, 14) in red and a filter to show only those rows. A side panel sets the 4 inputs and explains the outputs for that case.

tool.friction: 1) The worst problem is a silent failure. My first spec used `truth: {data: logic}` with logic.json, an object that holds `inputs` and `outputs`. Render printed "check ok", but the page showed a two-row key/value table of zeros ("0 of 2"). There was no error and no "fixed" line. I found it only because I took a screenshot. The truth component cannot read `inputs` and `outputs` from a data file, so I copied the three expressions and four input names into the spec. That goes against the rule "give the path, do not copy the data". `truth` should accept an `{inputs, outputs}` JSON object, for example `data: logic.json`, or render should give an error when the rows are not 0/1. 2) The graph colours nodes with `tone` by kind but draws no legend. I wrote the colour key by hand in a text node. 3) The graph cannot style an edge by a column. Power rails (VBAT, 3V3, 1V8) and signal or bus links look the same. The only edge style is `sign` (+/-), which is meant for causal loops. I wanted, for example, `edge_tone: {kind: power}` or a dashed style for power links. 4) Each dataset takes only one `join`. To get the domain of each end of a link, I had to chain two datasets (links_a, then links) with rename. It works but it is wordy. 5) The stats tile row cannot count truth-table rows. I could not put "alarm fires in 3 of 16 cases" in the summary at the top without working the number out by hand. The truth table shows "3 of 16" in its filter label only. 6) The order rule (summary first) conflicts with the brief. The reader needs the diagram and the truth table, and the only useful summary is blocks per domain. Render ran 3 times and printed no "fixed" or "error" lines. The last run printed "check ok".
